If you are comfortable with those ideas, you can choose a specific live-play preparation guide or an optional study task below. There is no requirement to start playing for money.

Revision, October 15, 2026: Connected the six stages to fresh practice and later review

Return later and explain a changed situation

At your next study session, close the lesson and try two checkpoint questions before reopening the explanation. Pick different situations on a later day. A possible routine is a short recall check at the next session and another later in the week; this is a practical suggestion, not a tested optimal schedule for poker.

  1. Recall: say the rule or question in your own words without looking.
  2. Change the example: use the checkpoint’s changed situation, not just the same answer letter.
  3. Repair one gap: follow the precise lesson link, then explain the difference.
  4. Keep one note: record the skill, the mistake and the link to return to. Pause when the task is done.

Use the six-stage study card for your own notes. It includes the route, guided-hand prompts and a later-review plan. Answers and progress are not sent to the website.

Why the course uses examples, explanations and return visits

The Institute of Education Sciences recommends combining worked examples with problem solving, asking for explanations, using retrieval practice and spacing study. Those general findings informed this design. They do not validate this poker course or establish a learning rate for its readers. Read the IES practice guide.

Poker mechanics were checked October 15, 2026 against PokerStars’ Hold’em rules and hand rankings. Their strategy suggestions are not adopted as answers to the scripted hand. External poker publishers may advertise gambling.

This is one route through standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em: actions and cards, preflop context, the flop, the river, ranges, then betting purpose. Each lesson begins with a limited first pass. Read those sections, explain the check below without the answer, then use a fresh situation to see what needs repair. The longer examples remain available as references.

Use a deck, counters or paper. No wager, playing account or purchase is needed. Begin with stage 1 when everything is new. You can pause anywhere or try the checkpoint first when you already know the mechanics

• Your first range

    Learn: separate known cards, physically possible hands and assumptions about their frequency. You do not need a chart or percentages for the first pass.

    Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown.

    Quick check: You hold A♥ J♥. Can the opponent hold A♥ Q♣? Does a check prove they are weak?

    Neither claim works. The exact A♥ Q♣ is impossible because your ace of hearts cannot be in two hands. Other legal hands remain possible, and a check does not establish their strength or frequency. Revisit known cards and possible hands if either possibility became a fact.

  • Betting with a purpose

    Learn: name which worse hands might call a value bet or which better hands might fold to a bluff. Compare a bet with checking when nothing is owed.

    Before moving on: describe the response you need, rather than using “I have a pair” or “I won the pot” as the whole argument.

    Quick check: Your bet makes every worse hand fold and every better hand call. Has “I have a pair” justified a value bet?

    No. Under that supplied response pattern, the worse hands do not pay and the better hands are the only callers. You still need to compare the bet with checking and examine the assumptions. This is a hypothetical response pattern, not a claim about actual players. Revisit worse hands that actually call.

For this scripted practice hand, you raise to 6 total and the small blind folds. The big blind already posted 2 on this betting round and faces your total wager of 6. The current pot is your 6, the folded small blind's 1 and the big blind's 2: 9.

  1. 1. Before the flop: follow the seats

    Six players start with 100 counters each. The small blind posts 1 and the big blind posts 2. There is no ante, fee or side pot. Three players fold. You are on the button, the seat marked by the dealer marker. Both blinds still have their first decisions.

    1. First seat: folded
    2. Next seat: folded
    3. Cutoff: folded
    4. Button: you
    5. Small blind: posted 1
    6. Big blind: posted 2

    98
    After your initial action on the button, who still has an initial decision?

    Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

    Explanation and a repair link

    The small blind and big blind still act. Before the flop, the initial action begins to the left of the big blind and proceeds clockwise. A raise can give earlier players another decision. The button is last in the initial order after the flop, not before it.

    A. Three folds do not finish the round. Both blinds still have decisions.

    B. Yes. The two seats after the button still have their initial decisions.

    C. The small blind still acts before the big blind. Its forced post was not its initial decision.

  2. 2. Preflop: add only what is missing

    For this scripted practice hand, you raise to 6 total and the small blind folds. The big blind already posted 2 on this betting round and faces your total wager of 6. The current pot is your 6, the folded small blind's 1 and the big blind's 2: 9.

    Your private cards

    A♥J♥

    Shared board

    No shared cards yet.
    Pot now
    9
    Your stack behind
    94
    Big blind behind
    98
    How many additional counters does the big blind need to call?

    Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

    Explanation and a repair link

    The call adds 6 - 2 = 4. The big blind's total contribution becomes 6. The pot then contains 6 + 1 + 6 = 13, and both remaining players have 94 behind. The folded small blind's counter stays in the pot. This explains the accounting, not whether either action is a good strategy.

    A. Six is the total wager. The big blind has already paid 2 of that total on this round.

    B. Adding the posted 2 to the total 6 counts those forced chips twice.

    C. Yes. Subtract the big blind's 2 already paid from the total wager of 6.

    Revisit the exact lesson section.

  3. 3. The flop: name what you have now

    The big blind calls. The flop, the first three shared cards, is jack of spades, seven of hearts and two of hearts. The big blind checks, meaning it makes no bet. Your private cards remain ace of hearts and jack of hearts.

    Your private cards

    A♥J♥

    Shared board

    J♠7♥2♥
    Pot now
    13
    Your stack behind
    94
    Big blind behind
    94
    Which description fits your cards on this flop?

    Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

    Explanation and a repair link

    Your current best five are J-J-A-7-2. You have a pair of jacks with an ace kicker, plus four hearts among your available cards. Another heart could complete a flush, but a possible improvement is not a completed hand or a guaranteed win. After the check you can check or bet; you do not call when nothing is owed.

    A. Yes. The two jacks make a pair; your two hearts plus two on the board make four hearts.

    B. A flush needs five hearts. Only four hearts are available to you now.

    C. The board's jack and your private jack already make a pair, even though you also have a draw.

    Revisit the exact lesson section.

  4. 4. A flop raise: count this round again

    The scripted line continues: you bet 4 and the big blind raises to 12 total on the flop. The pot is now the previous 13 plus your 4 plus the opponent's 12: 29. Your preflop contribution belongs to an earlier round.

    Your private cards

    A♥J♥

    Shared board

    J♠7♥2♥
    Pot now
    29
    Your stack behind
    90
    Big blind behind
    82

    Explanation and a repair link

    The call adds 12 - 4 = 8, making the pot 37. Each remaining player has put in 6 preflop and 12 on the flop, leaving 82 from the original 100. You may instead fold or make a legal raise; checking is unavailable against the unmatched wager. The accounting does not establish which choice is best.

    A. Twelve is the opponent's total flop wager. Your 4 on this round already pays part of it.

    B. Yes. Match 12 total after accounting for your 4 already paid on the flop.

    C. The raise is to 12 total, not by another 12 on top of your bet of 4.

    Revisit the exact lesson section.

  5. 5. The river: rebuild the hand

    You call the extra 8. The turn is nine of clubs; both players check, so nobody pays more on that round. The river is four of diamonds, the last shared card. The big blind bets 10 into the pot of 37, making the current pot 47.

    47

There is no universally correct action supplied here because the opponent's hidden hands and their frequencies have not been established.

    A. There are still only four hearts available, and an unmatched river bet prevents checking.

    B. The river is the fifth and final shared card. No later card will complete this missed draw.

    C. Yes. The missed flush leaves your pair, and no earlier-round payment covers this new bet.

    Optional after stage 4: if a call ends this heads-up cash-game hand, 10 / 57 is about 17.54%. With no fees or side pots this prices a call in chips; it does not measure your hand's equity or prove that calling is correct.

Your stack finishes at 129; the big blind has 72 and the folded small blind has 99. The three earlier folders still have 100 each. All six stacks sum to the original 600 counters.

    A. Yes. Your ace kicker wins, and receiving the pot includes getting back your own contributions.

    B. You receive 57, but 28 of it is your own earlier contribution. The net gain is 29.

    Learn: separate known cards, physically possible hands and assumptions about their frequency. You do not need a chart or percentages for the first pass.

    Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown.

    Quick check: You hold A♥ J♥. Can the opponent hold A♥ Q♣? Does a check prove they are weak?

    Neither claim works. The exact A♥ Q♣ is impossible because your ace of hearts cannot be in two hands. Other legal hands remain possible, and a check does not establish their strength or frequency. Revisit known cards and possible hands if either possibility became a fact.

  • Betting with a purpose

    Learn: name which worse hands might call a value bet or which better hands might fold to a bluff. Compare a bet with checking when nothing is owed.

    Before moving on: describe the response you need, rather than using “I have a pair” or “I won the pot” as the whole argument.

    Quick check: Your bet makes every worse hand fold and every better hand call. Has “I have a pair” justified a value bet?

    No. Under that supplied response pattern, the worse hands do not pay and the better hands are the only callers. You still need to compare the bet with checking and examine the assumptions. This is a hypothetical response pattern, not a claim about actual players. Revisit worse hands that actually call.
